label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses a large loss, as severe as you can justify (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS

  },

   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Arctic outbreak with NYC gas-constrained and the upstate-to-NYC transfer path congested, as in Winter Storm Elliott. Peak load runs 12% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.12), and Henry Hub rises 40% (gas_hh_pct 40). The main shock is the NYC minus WEST spread widening by $220/MWh for 7 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 220). It hits the 140 MW retail short in NYC (P5), which is unhedged against the spread beyond the WEST leg, and the higher load scales that loss up. P2 offsets about $0.9M, and the long WEST positions P1 and P4 gain about $0.4M from the load and gas moves. I add no extra WEST on-peak move, no DART shock and no spike days, so the loss comes from the zone-volume channel. The estimate scales the engine's winter P5 and P2 sensitivities linearly, so treat it as approximate.

scenario.narrative: A prolonged two-week cold spell, similar to January 2025, keeps NYC constrained. The NYC minus WEST spread stays $120/MWh wider than normal for 14 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 120), roughly the NYC-WEST day-ahead on-peak gap seen in January 2025. Load stays 15% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.15), which inflates the NYC retail obligation in P5. Henry Hub is up 60% (gas_hh_pct 60) and NY gas basis adds $15/MMBtu to the heat-rate call's fuel cost (ny_gas_basis_usd 15). The basis erases P4's gains from higher power prices. The long WEST swap P1 and the spread long P2 gain about $2M combined, but P5 loses far more because the shock lasts so long. There is no extra WEST price shock, no DART shock and no spike days, so the spread and load drive the loss. The loss is a linear extrapolation of the winter sensitivities and carries material uncertainty.

NYC is isolated behind transmission limits, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $300/MWh for 5 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 300), inside the winter historical maximum of 400.6. WEST is oversupplied and softens, so WEST on-peak falls a further 40% (ref_onpeak_pct -40), and real-time clears 30% below day-ahead (dart_pct -30). These two moves cost P1 about $0.3M. P3 gains only a little because it receives day-ahead minus real-time, so the result is a net loss from the DART shock. The dominant loss is still the P5 retail short in NYC, partly offset by P2. The mix is a WEST price drop plus a wide spread, unlike the other two scenarios. The estimate comes from the winter engine sensitivities scaled linearly, and no analogue fits this mix, so confidence is low.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long winter cold regime keeps NYC gas-constrained and the upstate-to-NYC transfer path tight. This is a slow grind, not a spike. The NYC minus WEST spread stays $70/MWh wider than normal for all 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70). That is a modest widening, well inside the winter historical range, but it accumulates over a long window. Load runs 6% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.06), which inflates the NYC retail obligation in P5. Henry Hub is up 15% (gas_hh_pct 15), which is consistent with a cold snap. The loss comes almost entirely from P5, the 140 MW NYC retail short, running around the clock for 30 days. P2 offsets about $1.3M. P1 and P4 gain roughly $0.8M from the load and gas moves. I add no extra WEST move, no DART shock and no spikes. The estimate scales the earlier engine results linearly in spread times days, so it is approximate.

scenario.narrative: A three-week cold regime in which NYC stays isolated while upstate gas-fired supply stays ample and imports are strong. The NYC minus WEST spread is $120/MWh wider for 21 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 120), and load is 10% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.10), which scales up the NYC retail obligation in P5. WEST on-peak softens a further 25% (ref_onpeak_pct -25), which cuts the gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. It also weakens the WEST leg that hedges P5. Gas is left unchanged (gas_hh_pct 0), so the cold is local to NYC load and constraints and the WEST price does not rise. There are no DART shocks and no spikes. The loss is dominated by P5. P2 offsets about $1.5M, and P1 is roughly flat because the load gain and the WEST drop cancel. The estimate scales the engine's winter sensitivities linearly in spread times days and is uncertain, and no analogue fits this mix.

A severe cold episode lasting 12 days with a gas squeeze and real-time stress, in the style of Winter Storm Elliott. The NYC minus WEST spread widens by $200/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 200), below the Elliott NYC minus WEST real-time spread of 338.5. Load is 15% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.15). Henry Hub is up 80% (gas_hh_pct 80) and NY gas basis adds $25/MMBtu to the cost of the heat-rate call (ny_gas_basis_usd 25), so P4 gives back its gains from higher power prices. Real-time clears 40% above day-ahead (dart_pct 40), which costs the WEST off-peak DART receipt P3. The shock also lifts WEST on-peak, so P1 gains about $1.3M. That gain partly offsets the large P5 loss from the wide NYC spread at high load. P2 gains about $1.4M. I use no spike days, because the winter spike sensitivity shows no effect. The loss estimate scales the engine's sensitivities linearly and is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long cold regime in which NYC stays transfer-constrained while WEST stays relatively well supplied. The NYC minus WEST spread is $95/MWh wider for all 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 95). This is the main driver, because the 140 MW NYC retail short (P5) runs around the clock and the loss accumulates over the full window. Load is 2% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.02), which scales P5 up slightly. Henry Hub is up 5% (gas_hh_pct 5), as expected in a cold snap, and NY gas basis adds $10/MMBtu to the heat-rate call (ny_gas_basis_usd 10), which erodes P4. WEST on-peak softens a further 30% (ref_onpeak_pct -30), which removes the gains on the long WEST swap P1. There are no spike days and no DART shock. P2 offsets about $1.7M. The loss estimate scales the earlier engine results linearly in spread times days and is approximate.

A 24-day cold regime in which NYC congestion persists and the real-time market clears below day-ahead on WEST because of a conservative day-ahead commitment. The NYC minus WEST spread is $110/MWh wider for 24 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 110), which drives the loss on the P5 retail short in NYC. Load is only 1% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.01), the minimum consistent with a cold snap, so the load channel is small. Real-time clears 50% below day-ahead (dart_pct -50). This lowers the WEST price path, so P1 and P4 lose the gains they would otherwise have. P3 gains a little from the DART receipt, so the DART shock is a net loss for the book. There are no gas, basis, WEST-only or spike shocks. P2 offsets about $1.6M. The estimate scales winter engine sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

A 15-day severe cold episode with high load and a sharply isolated NYC pocket. The NYC minus WEST spread is $170/MWh wider for 15 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 170), inside the winter historical range. Load runs 7% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.07), which scales up the P5 obligation. Henry Hub is up 25% (gas_hh_pct 25), consistent with a cold snap and the demand pull. WEST on-peak falls a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct -35) and real-time clears 20% below day-ahead (dart_pct -20), because upstate has surplus supply behind the constraint. These two moves cancel most of the gains P1 would otherwise earn from load and gas. The main loss is P5. P2 offsets about $1.5M. The estimate scales the winter engine sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS

- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.

2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.

4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).

scenario.narrative: A short, intense heat wave pushes N.Y.C. peak load to 1.12 times a typical summer day for 7 days. Downstate cooling load and transmission limits into Zone J widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $220/MWh on top of the base spread; the spread added is the shock, and the total stays inside the historical maximum of $289.7. The hit comes through P5, the N.Y.C. retail load obligation. It loses roughly $3,560 per $/MWh of spread per day at this load, or about $5.5M. P2, the long spread position, offsets about $0.9M, so the net congestion loss is about $4.6M. Higher load also lifts P1 and P4 by about $0.3M, giving a net loss of about $4.3M. WEST prices, gas, DART and spikes are left unshocked, so the loss comes only from the congestion and zone-volume channel. The June 2025 heat event is the analogue: N.Y.C. real-time on-peak was 625.5 against WEST at 416.5, a gap of about $209. The load ratio of 1.12 is not claimed from the analogue. The loss estimate is scaled linearly from the 5-day sensitivities, so confidence is only medium.

A 10-day heat dome holds daily peak load at 1.35 times a typical summer day, below the historical maximum of 1.514. Zone J is transmission-constrained and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $180/MWh. Upstate WEST has surplus hydro, wind and solar and cannot export. WEST on-peak prices therefore fall 35% relative to what load and gas imply, which removes much of the gain on the long positions P1 and P4. P5 is the main loss at about $7.7M, because the high load scales the retail obligation and the WEST hedge cannot keep pace. P2 offsets about $1.1M, and higher load and the weaker WEST price net out to about +$0.4M for P1 and P4 after the ref_onpeak_pct cut. The net loss is about $6M. Gas, DART and spike channels are left at zero. This scenario differs from S1 by combining high load with WEST weakness, so P1 and P4 stop hedging the zone-volume loss. The estimate extrapolates the 5-day sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

A two-week heat spell holds peak load at 1.25 times a typical summer day for 14 days. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $100/MWh wider than normal throughout, as downstate cooling demand persistently outruns import capability. WEST on-peak prices come in 25% below the gas and load implication because upstate supply is ample, which trims the gains on P1 and P4. NY gas basis rises $2/MMBtu on the P4 heat-rate call only, which lowers its payoff but cannot cost more than its base payoff. P5 loses about $5.6M over the 14 days. P2 gives back about $0.8M, so the net spread loss is about $4.7M. P1 and P4 gains from load, net of the WEST discount, and the small P6 loss together recover roughly $0.5M. The net loss is about $4.2M. The loss builds slowly from persistence, not from a single-day spike, so it differs from S1 and S2 in duration and path. No spike or DART shock is applied, because those would raise the long WEST positions more than they cost the short-option and DART positions. The estimate is scaled from 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long summer heat pattern (duration 30 days) keeps daily peak load at 1.05 times a typical day, a mild uplift that adds little to the long WEST hedges P1 and P4. Downstate cooling demand persistently outruns the transmission limit into Zone J, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $75/MWh wider than base on every one of the 30 days. The loss comes from zone volume: P5 is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price and loses about $3,300 per $/MWh of spread per day at normal load. That implies about $7.8M over 30 days at ratio 1.05. P2, the long spread position, offsets about $1.35M, and P1 plus P4 add about $0.5M from the higher load. The net loss is about $6M. Gas, WEST on-peak, DART and spikes are not shocked, so the book is hit only through the congestion and zone-volume channel. The spread is smaller than in the first round and lasts far longer, so the loss builds from persistence, not from one extreme day. The estimate scales the observed 7-day engine result for P5 and is uncertain.

A 30-day heat pattern (duration 30 days) lifts daily peak load to 1.10 times a typical day. Upstate WEST has surplus generation and limited export capacity, so WEST on-peak prices come in 50% below what load and gas imply (ref_onpeak_pct -50, inside the historical minimum of -88.5). That cuts the value of the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, so they no longer hedge the book. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $60/MWh wider on all 30 days because Zone J stays import-constrained. P5 loses about $6.6M on the wider spread at load ratio 1.10. P2 offsets about $1.1M. The WEST price drop costs P1 and P4 about $1.9M, and the load uplift returns about $1.0M, so they net about -$0.9M. The net loss is about $6.4M. Gas, DART and spike channels are unshocked. This differs from S4 because the WEST price drop turns the system and gas channels from hedges into losses. The pairing of falling WEST prices with a heat wave is unusual and the size is uncertain.

A 30-day heat pattern (duration 30 days) keeps daily peak load at 1.10 times a typical day. Henry Hub falls 25% because of a mild gas market (above the historical minimum of -44.2), which lowers WEST power prices and trims the gains on P1 and P4. A NY gas basis of $3/MMBtu is added to the gas price used by P4 only. It lowers the heat-rate call payoff and can never cost more than P4's base payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $70/MWh wider on all 30 days because Zone J is persistently import-constrained. P5 loses about $7.8M on the spread at load ratio 1.10. P2 offsets about $1.3M, and P1 plus P4 net close to zero to slightly positive, because the load gain roughly cancels the cheaper gas and the basis cost. The net loss is about $6M. WEST on-peak, DART and spike channels are unshocked. This differs from S4 and S5 by using gas and basis to weaken the power-long hedges, not a direct WEST price cut. The estimate extrapolates the 5-day sensitivities linearly and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day heat dome (duration 30 days) holds daily peak load at 1.25 times a typical summer day, inside the historical maximum of 1.514. Upstate WEST has surplus hydro, wind and solar and limited export capacity, so WEST on-peak prices clear 80% below what load and gas imply (ref_onpeak_pct -80, inside the historical minimum of -88.5). That nearly erases the value of the long WEST swap P1 and pushes the heat-rate call P4 out of the money, so the power-long hedges turn into losses of about $1.7M and $0.65M. Zone J stays import-constrained and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $60/MWh wider on all 30 days. P5 loses about $7.8M on the wider spread at load ratio 1.25. P2 offsets about $1.1M. Gas, DART and spikes are not shocked. This differs from earlier rounds in the size of the WEST price cut and the higher load. The estimate scales the engine's earlier 30-day P5 and P1 results linearly and is uncertain, because a heat wave with deeply discounted WEST prices is an unusual combination.

A 30-day heat pattern (duration 30 days) lifts daily peak load to 1.15 times a typical day. Henry Hub falls 40% in a weak gas market (gas_hh_pct -40, above the historical minimum of -44.2). That drags WEST power down and cancels most of the load gain on the long swap P1, which ends near zero. A NY gas basis of $5/MMBtu is added to the gas price used by P4 only. It pushes the heat-rate call to its floor, so P4 loses roughly its base payoff of about $0.5M. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $90/MWh wider on all 30 days because Zone J is persistently import-constrained. P5 loses about $10.7M on the spread at load ratio 1.15. P2 offsets about $1.6M. WEST on-peak, DART and spike channels are unshocked. The path is slow and driven by persistence. It combines a spread loss with a cheap-gas hedge failure, unlike earlier rounds that cut WEST directly. The estimate is extrapolated from engine results for P5, P2 and P1 and is uncertain.

A 30-day heat pattern (duration 30 days) leaves daily peak load only slightly above normal at 1.03 times a typical day, so the long WEST positions P1 and P4 gain almost nothing from load. Local N.Y.C. constraints keep Zone J cut off from upstate supply, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $100/MWh wider on all 30 days. P5, the short N.Y.C. retail obligation, loses about $10.7M on the spread. P2 offsets about $1.8M. WEST on-peak prices clear 30% below the load and gas implication (ref_onpeak_pct -30) because upstate supply is ample, so P1 loses about $0.6M and P4 about $0.3M. Gas, DART and spikes are unshocked. This is the congestion-dominated case, with a much larger spread than earlier rounds and almost no load uplift, so the loss comes almost entirely from zone volume. The spread of $100 sits well above anything seen as a 30-day average, so the shock is severe and the estimate, scaled linearly from engine results, is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

The WEST discount turns the long hedges P1 and P4 into losses of about $1.25M and $0.5M. Gas, DART and spikes are unshocked. This is larger than earlier rounds because the spread is wider and persists for the full horizon. The estimate scales engine results from earlier rounds and is uncertain.

A 15-day intense heat dome (duration 15 days) lifts daily peak load to 1.30 times a typical summer day, inside the historical maximum of 1.514. Downstate cooling demand overwhelms import capability into Zone J, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $200/MWh wider than base on all 15 days, below the historical maximum of $289.7 in total. The high load scales up the retail obligation P5, which loses about $13.6M. P2 offsets about $1.8M. WEST on-peak prices clear 40% below the load and gas implication (ref_onpeak_pct -40) because upstate supply cannot reach downstate. That turns P1 and P4 into losses of about $0.55M and $0.25M, even with the load uplift. Gas, DART and spikes are not shocked. Compared with S10, this scenario is shorter and has higher load, so the loss comes from load times spread, not from duration. The estimate is scaled from engine results and is uncertain.

A 30-day heat pattern (duration 30 days) lifts daily peak load to 1.15 times a typical summer day. Henry Hub falls 40% in a weak gas market (gas_hh_pct -40, above the historical minimum of -44.2), which drags WEST power down and cancels the load gain on the long swap P1. A NY gas basis of $8/MMBtu is added to the gas price used by P4 only, which pushes the heat-rate call to its floor, so P4 loses about its base payoff of about $0.45M. WEST on-peak also clears 30% below the gas and load implication (ref_onpeak_pct -30), which costs P1 about $0.7M. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $140/MWh wider on all 30 days because Zone J stays import-constrained. P5 loses about $16.8M at load ratio 1.15, and P2 offsets about $2.5M. DART and spikes are unshocked. This combines a hedge failure through cheap gas with a larger spread than in S8. The estimate scales engine results and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: Winter gas-supply scenario. A pipeline constraint into the NYC area, with Z6 gas trading at a large premium, forces N.Y.C. generators onto oil or limited gas for 10 days. Henry Hub rises 40% (gas_hh_pct=40) and the NY gas basis adds $40/MMBtu to P4's gas cost only (ny_gas_basis_usd=40), which cuts P4's payoff. Load peaks 5% above normal (load_peak_ratio=1.05). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $300/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd=300), which is inside the historical maximum of 400.6. That widening is the main loss: P5 (short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load) loses about $3.7k per $/MWh per day, and P2 recovers only about $0.6k. No extra WEST on-peak move, no DART shock and no spike are applied. The WEST price gains on P1 and P4 from higher gas and load partly offset the loss. Estimate from the winter sensitivities, scaled linearly: spread about -$9.3M, other channels about +$0.4M, net about -$8.9M. The sensitivities were run at 5 days and the winter spike entry is zero, so the estimate is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: Winter gas-supply scenario lasting 21 days. Henry Hub rises 80% (gas_hh_pct=80), but constrained downstate delivery lifts the N.Y.C. premium. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $180/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd=180), which is the main loss through P5. Upstate WEST has relatively ample gas and surplus imports. As a result its on-peak price rises 15% less than gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct=-15), which hurts the long P1 swap and the heat-rate call P4. Gas cost to P4 rises by $20/MMBtu through the NY basis (ny_gas_basis_usd=20). Load stays at a normal 1.0 times peak with no large-load shock, DART is unshocked and there are no spike days. Estimate from the winter sensitivities, scaled linearly: spread about -$11.7M, WEST discount about -$0.6M, gas gains on P1 and P4 about +$1.0M, net about -$11M. I am unsure the sensitivities scale linearly over 21 days, and gas up with WEST relatively soft is only moderately consistent.

scenario.narrative: Winter gas-supply scenario: a severe 7-day supply failure (freeze-offs and pipeline curtailments) at the Winter Storm Elliott scale, with N.Y.C. gas-fired units short of fuel. Henry Hub rises 150% (gas_hh_pct=150, inside the historical maximum of 725.6) and the NY gas basis adds $60/MMBtu to P4's cost (ny_gas_basis_usd=60). Load is 12% above normal (load_peak_ratio=1.12, below the historical maximum of 1.196), which raises the P5 load multiplier. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $380/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd=380), below the historical maximum of 400.6. That is the dominant loss on P5, only partly offset by P2. No extra WEST move, no DART shock and no spike are added, because those would mostly help the long WEST positions. Estimate from the winter sensitivities, scaled linearly: spread about -$8.2M, load about -$0.2M, gains on P1 and P4 from higher gas and load about +$0.7M, net about -$7.7M. The scaling is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Winter gas-supply scenario lasting 25 days. A prolonged downstate pipeline constraint keeps N.Y.C. fuel costs high, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $120/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd=120). That is far below the 400.6 historical maximum and is held for the whole 25 days, so the loss comes from duration rather than a one-day extreme. P5 (short 140 MW of N.Y.C. load, 24 h) loses about $3.4k per $/MWh per day and P2 recovers only about $0.6k of that. Henry Hub rises 30% (gas_hh_pct=30) and the NY gas basis adds $10/MMBtu to P4's gas cost only (ny_gas_basis_usd=10). Upstate WEST has relatively ample supply, so its on-peak price is 25% below what gas implies (ref_onpeak_pct=-25). That hurts the long P1 swap and the WEST leg of the P5 hedge. Load, DART and spikes are not shocked, because they would mostly lift the long WEST positions. Rough estimate from the winter sensitivities, scaled linearly: P5 about -$11.6M, P2 about +$1.8M, P1 about -$0.1M, P4 about -$0.2M, net about -$10M. The linear scaling over 25 days is uncertain.

Winter gas-supply scenario lasting the full 30 days. Cold weather coincides with a gas supply shortfall. Load is 8% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio=1.08, well inside the 1.196 historical maximum), which scales up the P5 obligation. Henry Hub rises 10% (gas_hh_pct=10) and the NY gas basis adds $15/MMBtu to P4's cost only (ny_gas_basis_usd=15). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $90/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd=90) for all 30 days. A moderate spread held for a month limits the historical implausibility. WEST on-peak is 30% below the level that gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct=-30), because imports and upstate supply are ample. That erodes P1 and the WEST leg of the P5 hedge, and the load uplift offsets part of the P1 loss. No DART shock and no spike are applied, because they would mostly help the long WEST positions. Rough estimate from the winter sensitivities, scaled linearly: P5 about -$12.1M, P2 about +$1.6M, P1 and P4 about -$0.2M combined, net about -$10.5M. The uncertainty is large because the effects are not additive.

Winter gas-supply scenario lasting 30 days. Gas is trapped upstate behind a constrained path to N.Y.C., so WEST on-peak is 60% below what gas implies (ref_onpeak_pct=-60, inside the -93.2 historical minimum). That hurts the long P1 swap, takes P4 out of the money, and cuts the value of the WEST hedge in P5, which is long WEST at H=34.05. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $100/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd=100), well below the 400.6 historical maximum, because downstate stays short of gas. Henry Hub rises only 5% (gas_hh_pct=5), since the stress is regional rather than national. There is no load shock, no DART shock, no basis shock and no spike. The loss is a long, moderate squeeze that works through zone volume (P5) and the system channel (P1). Rough estimate from the winter sensitivities, scaled linearly: P5 about -$14M, P2 about +$1.8M, P1 about -$1.5M, P4 about -$0.3M, net about -$13M or more. I have low confidence in the size, because the WEST price level used to scale the hedge loss is inferred.

scenario.narrative: Large upstate and downstate loads arrive about 1,500 MW slower than the Gold Book (large_load_shock_mw -1500, near the stated low-shortfall range), so the summer peak ratio falls to 0.97. WEST is oversupplied and its on-peak price softens a further 20% (ref_onpeak_pct -20). N.Y.C. stays tight because of local reliability needs and limited transfer into Zone J, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh for the full 30 days (the spread gets the largest weight). The main loss is P5, the short 140 MW N.Y.C. retail load that is hedged only at WEST. P2 gains only about a fifth of that, since it is 25 MW against 140 MW. P1 and P4 lose a little from the weaker WEST price. Gas, DART and spikes are left at zero. The estimate scales the engine's 5-day sensitivities linearly, which is uncertain, and a spread this wide for 30 days is beyond history, so confidence is low.

Large-load arrivals fall 1,500 MW short (large_load_shock_mw -1500) and the peak ratio drops to 0.95, so about 5% less load clears in summer. With surplus upstate supply, the WEST on-peak price falls a further 75% (ref_onpeak_pct -75), which is inside the historical minimum of -88.5%, for the full 30 days. The loss is a system-level price loss. P1 is long 100 MW at K1 = 39.49 and pays out against a base price of about $53, and it loses heavily when WEST falls. P4's heat-rate call loses its base payoff because WEST ends below 8 x gas + 3. P6 earns only its small premium. Spread, gas basis, DART and spikes are zero, so P5 and P2 are not hit. The loss is smaller than in the congestion scenarios, and the figure scales the engine sensitivities linearly. It is also uncertain whether the swap settles on 22 weekdays or on all 30 days.

A 1,500 MW large-load shortfall (large_load_shock_mw -1500, peak ratio 0.95) combines three adverse channels for 20 days. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $120/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 120), because downstate stays tight while WEST is long supply, and this hurts the unmatched P5 retail load. WEST on-peak falls a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct -35), which hurts P1 and P4. A $6/MMBtu basis on the gas price used by P4 (ny_gas_basis_usd 6) removes the rest of P4's base payoff. This is a high-gas-cost, low-power-price mix. Henry Hub, DART and spikes are left at zero. The P5 loss is partly offset by the long 25 MW spread position P2, so the net loss is below that of the 30-day congestion scenario. The estimate comes from scaling the 5-day sensitivities linearly, so confidence is low.

TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses a large loss, as severe as you can justify (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: large_load_shortfall
Season: summer


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):
{
 "active_positions": [
  "P1",
  "P2",
  "P3",
  "P4",
  "P5",
  "P6"
 ],
 "book": [
  {
   "channel": "system",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price is above K1",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak price is below K1",
   "position": "P1",
   "what": "Long 100 MW swap on the WEST on-peak price, strike K1 = 39.49 $/MWh, 16 h per on-peak weekday"
  },
  {
   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",
   "what": "Retail load obligation: short 140 MW x (load / normal load) in N.Y.C. at fixed price R = 45.65, hedged by a long WEST position at H = 34.05, 24 h; P&L = (R - N.Y.C. price) + (WEST price - H), times load"
  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios with a large loss with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive 500 MW slower than the Gold Book (large_load_shock_mw -500, the near-term high end of the shortfall range). The load ratio stays at 1.0, so the N.Y.C. retail obligation in P5 keeps close to full size and the loss is not reduced by lower load. Downstate stays tight with limited transfer into Zone J, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $100/MWh for all 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100). That is far below the earlier $150 case. The short 140 MW N.Y.C. load in P5 loses roughly $3,300/MWh-day per $1 of spread, and the long 25 MW spread in P2 offsets about a fifth of it. With less load than expected, real-time clears 40% below day-ahead (dart_pct -40), which cuts the WEST price that P1 and P4 settle on. P3 gains slightly. WEST on-peak, gas and spikes are left at zero. The estimate scales the engine's 5-day sensitivities linearly and ignores non-additivity, so confidence is low.

A 800 MW shortfall of large-load arrivals (large_load_shock_mw -800, near the 2030 shortfall of -900) leaves WEST oversupplied. N.Y.C. stays constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread blows out by $200/MWh, but only for a short 14-day hot stretch (pocket_minus_ref_usd 200, duration_days 14). This is the congestion channel and it drives the loss through P5, partly offset by the 25 MW long spread in P2. WEST on-peak falls a further 40% (ref_onpeak_pct -40) because of surplus upstate supply, which hurts the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. The load ratio stays at 1.0 so that P5 keeps near full size. Gas, DART and spikes are zero. The spread is near the historical maximum of 289.7, so the scenario is probably flagged as implausible. The loss estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities, so confidence is low.

A 900 MW large-load shortfall (large_load_shock_mw -900, the 2030 shortfall) creates a broad surplus lasting 30 days. WEST on-peak falls a further 60% (ref_onpeak_pct -60), inside the historical minimum of -88.5%, which hits the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 (system and gas channels). Real-time clears 70% below day-ahead (dart_pct -70), which lowers the settlement price again and also moves P3. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by a modest $70/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70) because downstate still needs local generation, and this drives P5 and P2 (zone-volume and congestion). The load ratio stays at 1.0 so that P5 keeps its size. Gas and spikes are zero. P1 and P4 losses are bounded, since WEST cannot fall below zero, and P5 supplies most of the loss. The effects are not additive, so the figure is a rough linear scaling of the sensitivities and confidence is low.
